title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
description: A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home
body: A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire. Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government."So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives, and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels. Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

schema.headline: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington

title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Newman will head to Australia with Harry Styles next month after more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Mancheste
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Newman will head to Australia with Harry Styles next month after more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and ManchesterByPaul Glynn & Mark SavageFast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.During her opening night in Brixton, Newman debuted her new song Survival and was also joined by fellow London soul-pop singer Gabrielle for a duet of her 1993 hit Dreams.Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.Figure caption, Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.But after three more gigs this weekend and an extra date next weekend, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her."Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me."I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."'Big shoes to fill'Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC."The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted."No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill."But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."After more gigs in Brixton, Brighton and Manchester, she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles next month for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked"."'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request."It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zayn were my favourites."So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

schema.headline: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run

title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup 2026: Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won
description: Sharks and ladders played their part in England's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup success.As they chased success in Australia, they had a ladder in
body: Sharks and ladders played their part in England's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup success.As they chased success in Australia, they had a ladder in team meetings to help them visualise their route to the trophy - spray painting a rung gold with each victory.And they spent time comparing themselves to lifeguards and sharks. It was all part of coach Tom Coyd's masterplan, which boiled down to one thing - taking an aggressive approach. It worked. On Friday, they beat France 50-38 in the World Cup final in Wollongong, to defend the trophy they won in Manchester four years ago.Not that Coyd ever used the word 'defend'. He has steered clear of that term since England lifted the trophy in November 2022. For four years, he has wanted his team to have a more attacking mindset in the pursuit of back-to-back world titles.His team were positive from the off at this tournament, amassing 386 points across the group stage and semi-finals while conceding just 68.And his approach ultimately ensured that England became the first nation to win the Wheelchair World Cup three times."I think your reality is the story that you tell yourself," Coyd said. "And the narrative that we felt might be upon us coming in was that we are here to defend and we are here to retain."We found that framing to be defensive, to be a bit passive - and knowing that we've been world number one since November 2022, we wanted to come in with an attacking mindset and with a hunter's mindset. "If we had not spent the last four years talking about defending the World Cup, we weren't going to spend the last three weeks [at this tournament] talking about it either. "We wanted to prime the group to be forward thinking, to attack the attack when we didn't have the ball - and when we did have the ball, to be a shark smelling blood in the water." Across the World Cup finals of 2013, 2017 and 2022, the game's two powerhouse nations had been separated by a total of only 10 points - two in the first match, and four in the following two.However, on the western coast of Australia - around 70 miles south of where England won the inaugural competition in Sydney back in 2008 - Coyd's group of players served up an exceptional display.  Having initially forged ahead, England then fought back from a 22-10 deficit before powering to victory against Cyril Torres' uncompromising French side. "I think the way they executed tonight was just outstanding," Coyd added.  "I don't think France have moved backwards. If anything, they looked hungrier than I've ever seen them."But the rate of which these 10 lads have moved on just blew my mind. I'm so proud of them."Thirty minutes into the final, England were in danger of disappointment. France, having trailed 10-0, had responded with 22 unanswered points to take control. However, that dominance was fleeting. By the break, tries from Rob Hawkins - recently crowned the world's best player for a third time - and Jack Brown had restored order. And when captain Lewis King led a short half-time huddle, it delivered a moment of reassurance for the group that quietly helped lay the platform for success. "Lewis' presence is everything for this team," added Coyd."He always finds the right words at the right time. That's before, during and after games. "Even in those moments during the match today, where we've been calling it a riptide - continuing on a surfing theme, when it feels like the waves are going against you, even though you feel like you don't deserve that. "The steadiness and the composure that Lewis just lives and breathes so innately - the boys feed off of it. He's without the doubt the talisman for this group."Joe Coyd - the head coach's younger brother, who scored four of England's nine tries - added: "We don't need a massive rousing 'let's all go together' type of speech. "We've got such confidence in each other and we've all seen the work we're doing and we challenge each other in such a good, positive way."Tom's not even [been] in the changing room in the last messages today and hasn't been all tournament."Jack Brown, playing at his fifth World Cup and earning his third winner's medal, added: "I don't think the team missed that [not having a rousing speech] because we saw it as a confidence in the team. "We knew what we had to do and we knew that we had so many leaders in our team."

schema.headline: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup 2026: Sharks, ladders and a four-year plan - how England won

title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
description: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatUpdated 4 hours agoSpanish
body: Image source, EPAImage caption, Rosalía released her fourth album Lux last year to rave reviews ByRiyah CollinsBBC NewsbeatUpdated 4 hours agoSpanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux. The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc. The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, After a career spanning three decades, Daddy Yankee was recognised with a lifetime achievement awardIt was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution"."It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Diljit Dosanjh became the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin GrammysAccepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far"."Long live Argentine folk music," he added.Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.Additional reporting by Abu Bakar YasinListen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

schema.headline: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys

title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
description: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US presiden
body: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?The answer is very.The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president. US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China. On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny. Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.Now the political pressure is building.Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

schema.headline: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House

title: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?
description: Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property l
body: Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, The images Olivia Nicole saw of a home on Rightmove (l) were completely different to how the property looked in real life (r)ByDaniel ThomasBBC NewsHave you ever been impressed by the pictures of a property on an estate agent's website, only to find the place looks completely different when you view it in person?Then there's a chance that AI was used to enhance the images you saw.From repainted walls to imaginary lawns, estate agents are increasingly using the technology to make homes seem more appealing, arguing it helps buyers visualise the potential of a place. But experts warn it can go too far and mislead prospective buyers - a trend dubbed "housefishing". So how much AI enhancement is too much? 'The rooms were much smaller'Earlier this year Olivia Nicole, 29, was searching online for five-bedroom properties in south-west London when a house on Rightmove caught her eye.But when she arrived to view it several days later she initially thought she had come to the wrong place. "The rooms were much smaller than they were in the pictures and the decor was totally different," she tells the BBC. "Some structural features were also different."For example, there was a raised section of the wall behind the sofa that didn't appear in the images. The windows were also noticeably smaller. Olivia was so surprised she took her own pictures of the property for comparison.Image source, Winkworth/SuppliedImage caption, AI has been used to make the property look more luxuriousIt later turned out the pictures she had seen on Rightmove, which also appeared on the Zoopla and Winkworth websites, were enhanced with AI. But that wasn't clear in the listing, Olivia says, and she feels the agent wasted her time. "It was frustrating, because I had taken several hours off work for the viewing which I had to make up for." All three companies told the BBC they had strict guidelines on how AI could be used on their websites and have since taken the images down. 'A surge of AI listings'Estate agents have long used wide-angle lens cameras or Photoshop to make homes seem bigger or more appealing to buyers, but AI is making this process much easier and more accessible. It is difficult to quantify how common the practice is, says the Guild of Property Professionals, a trade group of independent estate agents, but it has issued guidance on how to use AI enhancement responsibly. According to a recent survey, external of 906 UK homebuyers, one in five who had who purchased a home in the past year said they had viewed a property where the listing photos had been digitally enhanced to make the home appear better than it actually was.Jack Bushrod reviews quirky property listings he finds on Rightmove for his social media channel, Housing Horrors, and says he has seen a "surge" of AI-enhanced images over the last six months.He thinks using AI is fine up to a point - to declutter a busy room, or add furniture to an empty one so a prospective buyer can see its potential. But he draws the line at anything that misleads a prospective buyer or wastes their time. "I've seen one house where they had removed a pillar and added a window. Others might use AI to remove stains on the carpet or cracks in tiles. It's little details you would only notice in person." He says most of the enhanced images he's seen weren't clearly labelled as AI-generated.Image source, Howards/SuppliedImage caption, Cara says AI was used to empty her son's room in the image on the left Cara, 38, is currently selling her home in Lowestoft, Suffolk, and says she was surprised when she saw the AI-enhanced pictures of her property her estate agent, Howards, put on Rightmove. In one photo, her son's room was completely emptied of toys and clutter. In another, of her daughter's room, the agent appears to have removed a doll's house, brightened the room, and used AI to change the shape of a rug, but that image has since been taken down.Cara has had several viewings so far and says that one person has commented on the differences. But she says she trusts Howards, which has acknowledged the use of AI in the property listing. "If they'd changed something structurally or it was really wild and didn't look like our home at all then I would put my foot down," she says.Image source, Howards/SuppliedImage caption, In one picture (l), the AI removed a doll's house and changed the shape of a rug  A spokeswoman told the BBC that Howards had now introduced a policy of labelling all AI-enhanced photos. She added that the firm never used AI "to misrepresent the fundamental features of a property". "It's about helping people imagine the possibilities, not changing the reality of what's being sold."'Jumping on the bandwagon'Trading Standards told the BBC that estate agents can use AI to make basic enhancements to photos, or to virtually furnish an empty room or garden, as long as they indicate they have used the technology. But it says structurally changing a room, for example by adding a window, or hiding features could mislead consumers and break the law.Jack Bushrod thinks all estate agents should have to clearly label AI-enhanced photos and mention any use of the tech prominently in the key features slide of a property listing. He also expects to see more housefishing as time goes on.  "My worry is the more estate agents use AI, others will see the trend and jump on the bandwagon."Additional reporting by Star McFarlaneGet our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: The rise of 'housefishing' - when does using AI go from enhancing to misleading?

title: Pectus excavatum: 'My deformity left me feeling invisible'
description: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw meImage caption, Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made he
body: My physical deformity left me feeling invisible - but one surgeon saw meImage caption, Charlie kept her condition hidden for years and says it made her life "hell" at timesByHealth correspondent, BBC News NIAs a teenager at school, Charlie Clarke "felt awful" in her uniform, with a physical deformity leaving her so self-conscious that she hid from her classmates.At home, she wrapped her dressing gown tight around her chest, hoping it would conceal her condition - and didn't even tell her parents about it.Now 26, Charlie has lived with pectus excavatum - a congenital chest wall condition that can make the chest appear sunken or hollow - for years.As she awaits surgical treatment, she said the emotional and physical effects of the condition were "unimaginable and unignorable"."Having pectus excavatum, which is a disability and a deformity under my shirt, was at times hell," she said.Her worst memories from her teenage years are of hiding in the school bathroom during PE so other girls would not comment on her having "four breasts"."I got to a point where I felt awful wearing my school uniform because of how I looked, also because of how people looked at me and made comments about my chest," said Charlie, from County Down.Image source, Charlie ClarkeImage caption, Charlie didn't tell her parents about the severity of her condition for yearsThe condition, which affects one in every 200 people, means Charlie's heart and lungs are compressed, which triggers breathlessness and an increased heart rate that can cause her to lose consciousness.Charlie is one of 85 people in Northern Ireland who are waiting for surgery for pectus conditions.Many of them have been waiting for their operation for less than two years - but five have been on the list for longer than five years.The Department of Health said it acknowledged that some patients in Northern Ireland "have endured lengthy waits", adding that the volume of patients combined with "other demands on the thoracic surgery service have contributed to pressures on waiting times".But it said it had secured extra funding for more surgeries in order to reduce the amount of people on the waiting list, resulting in additional pectus procedures in the last three years.It also said it had agreed a further proposal "which should help to reduce both the number of patients waiting and the length of their waits". 'I was misdiagnosed'If diagnosed early, patients can often be treated without surgery.But getting that early diagnosis is key - and treatment depends on the type of pectus, how severe it is and the patient's age.Charlie said she was previously "misdiagnosed, including [being] told I had anxiety"."It wasn't until I had my shirt off in front of a clinical technician and she said they were unable to see my heart in a scan, it was compressed, and only then was I referred to a thoracic surgeon."That was when she was 23 years old, which is considered too old for non-surgical treatment.Image source, Charlie ClarkeImage caption, Charlie wants to raise awareness of the conditionA breakthrough came when Charlie met someone who truly understood her experience.Niall McGonigle, a Northern Ireland-based consultant thoracic surgeon, specialises in chest wall deformities.What makes his expertise particularly unique is that he suffered from a pectus deformity himself as a child and underwent surgery at 17."I was called freak and a mutant at school," he said."It drove me away from sports because of changing for PE - I was bullied."It is what started my interest in medicine... I was profoundly interested in surgery and specifically pectus."McGonigle said the condition was not recognised in Northern Ireland, and patients are often dismissed as asking for cosmetic surgery, which is not the case.Image source, Niall McGonigleImage caption, Niall McGonigle was inspired to become a surgeon after his experience with a pectus deformity"There is a lot of evidence to show there are restrictions on the lungs and heart, which can be debilitating," he said."If this is diagnosed early, patients can be treated with non-surgical services."But Northern Ireland doesn't provide this and our young people are having to go to England instead."McGonigle said Northern Ireland's limited pectus surgery service had been undermined by inconsistent funding.Charlie's surgery will involve two metal bars being placed in her chest and a metal plate in her sternum, allowing her heart and lungs to return to their natural positions.She said she was speaking out to raise awareness of the condition and to help others who have it, including her 11-year-old sister."I don't want her to have to wait this long and for her life to be paused and for her condition to become life-threatening," Charlie said.What is pectus excavatum?Pectus excavatum, also known as "funnel chest", is different for everyone. Most who have the condition were born with it.A patient's breastbone curves inwards, with a dip the ribs, which can leave the chest appearing sunken or hollow.It is usually more noticeable in childhood or teenage years.One treatment is vacuum bell therapy, using a suction device that sits over the sunken part of the chest to gradually lift the breastbone forwards.It works best in younger people with a flexible chest wall and a relatively shallow deformity.Another treatment, compression bracing, involves a specially fitted brace and is most effective in teenagers - but generally less so once the chest becomes rigid in adulthood.In its statement, the Department of Health said work it carried out in 2023 led to the commissioning of a service for "non-surgical bracing of pectus carinatum".It added it is understood this "can, in appropriately selected patients, negate the requirement for surgery"."The impact of this service will be evaluated, including its potential to free up theatre capacity for those conditions which can only be resolved surgically."Image caption, Vacuum bell therapy is a non-surgical treatment that works best for younger peopleLast month, patients and health professionals from across the UK met in Belfast to discuss the condition.Simon Kendall, of the charity Pectus Matters, said early treatment saves the health service money in the long term."If you get that treatment when the patient is young and chest wall is more flexible you can avoid the big operations in the future."

schema.headline: Pectus excavatum: 'My deformity left me feeling invisible'

title: Bruno Fernandes rejects second Manchester United contract offer
description: In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.It is usual for the first, second and someti
body: In theory, the current contract stand-off between Manchester United and Bruno Fernandes is not a big deal.It is usual for the first, second and sometimes quite a few more offers to be rejected as part of the rough and tumble of negotiations.United do have the option to trigger an option to add an extra year. However, there is reason why both sides might be wary to commit beyond that at this stage.On Fernandes' part, there is a clear desire to compete for the biggest prizes. He can see the best years of his career drifting away. Yet again United have failed to build on a season of promise and he will now be wanting to see what impact Mauricio Pochettino has when he eventually arrives from the United States.Fernandes was coveted by the Saudi Pro League 18 months ago, although the feeling has been he would prefer to stay in Europe.On United's side, they will have noted Fernandes' alarming drop-off from the levels he hit last season, when he broke the Premier League assists record and won all the major player of the year honours.Liverpool committed a huge amount of money to Mohamed Salah's last contract and that turned out to be a heavy financial burden. United will not want to get saddled with a major contract over an extended period for an underperforming player.

schema.headline: Bruno Fernandes rejects second Manchester United contract offer

title: Formula 1's diamond 'heist': an unsolved mystery?
description: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula
body: Where were you between the hours of 1pm and 3pm on 23 May 2004?If you were in Monaco, consider yourself a suspect - or at least a witness - in Formula 1's biggest unsolved mystery.A $300,000 diamond was last seen stuck to the front of an F1 car before it crashed on the first lap of the Grand Prix and it still has not been found 22 years later.Did someone pick it up? Was it swept up with all the debris? Did it slip down a drain? Was it even a real diamond?Someone, somewhere, knows something.The reason why a 1.4 carat diamond was attached to the most delicate part of a car that reaches 200mph in a race was straightforward: publicity.Jaguar Racing's results on the track had been mediocre at best since becoming an F1 team in 2000 and by 2004 its parent company Ford had decided it would be pulling them out of the sport."My job flipped from primarily running the team to primarily selling the team and finding a new owner or they would shut it down," former team principal Tony Purnell tells BBC Sport."It was probably the worst year of my life. Particularly because for the first few months I was sworn to secrecy."His team needed some good PR to divert attention away from performance and improve its appeal.They had enjoyed a successful promotional weekend in Silverstone the previous season thanks to a tie-up with Terminator 3 and so director of communications Nav Sidhu was looking to recreate the magic with another bit of help from a movie."I'd heard on the grapevine, around about the winter of 2003, that they were making Ocean's Twelve and we discovered that they were shooting some of the scenes in Monte Carlo," Sidhu says."One thing led to another and before you knew it, we had agreed [a deal] with George Clooney, Brad Pitt and Matt Damon."Sidhu had arranged with legendary Hollywood producer Jerry Weintraub to have the film's branding and stars take over the team for the Monaco weekend.The film plot centred on an audacious theft of a diamond-encrusted Faberge egg. Sidhu decided he wanted some sparkle on his cars too at the most glamorous race in the F1 calendar.Sidhu negotiated with diamond company Steinmetz that the two Jaguar cars would have gems - which would today be worth about $1m in total - attached to them.What happened next, though, was not part of the script.While the champagne corks were popping on nearby mega yachts in the principality, the diamonds were being hand-delivered into the garages. There were two that would be mounted on to the car and a larger gem just for the photos.The diamonds for the cars were encased by steel and fixed to the nose cones. One on experienced driver Mark Webber's car and one on rookie Christian Klien's.Webber was starting from 11th place in the grid and Klien - in only his sixth race - was starting from 14th. They weren't expected to challenge for the podium, but they were expected to bring the diamonds back.Monaco's street circuit is demanding, with narrow roads, tight turns and a tunnel.Overtaking is difficult and crashes are common - as Klien soon found out.In a chaotic first lap, the Austrian made contact with one of the Jordan cars exiting the Mirabeau corner. This damaged the front of his car - where the diamond was - and led to a slow collision with the barriers at the famous Loews hairpin.Klien climbed out unhurt but the front of the car was crumpled.It was not long before Sidhu had the diamond company on the phone asking if they would get their diamond back."I can't remember what I answered, but it certainly wasn't 'yes'," he says.He couldn't even get on to the track to have a look as the race had another 76 laps to go and only then would the car - which had been lifted off the track by a crane and left behind the barriers - return to the garage."I was consumed with getting to that spot as quickly as I possibly could," Sidhu says."That hour and a half waiting for the race to finish felt like a day and a half, every single lap was just like pulling teeth."By the time he had the chance to have a look, there was no sign of the diamond.But there were plenty of theories.Theory: it was not a real diamondSidhu completely denies the rumours of a fake diamond."I've learned that any diamond company is not going to go out there, particularly in the public domain, and use fake diamonds because clearly there's a high risk of being caught," he says."Had we used a fake diamond in that car and what took place took place, then clearly the embarrassment and the disrepute it would bring Jaguar, and Formula 1 for that matter, was too high risk."There's been loads of conspiracy theories about was it a real diamond or was Christian told to crash his car and I think that's what's given the story its life - there's a mystery to this story and that mystery will always breed different theories."Purnell backs up the legitimacy of the diamond, recalling a conversation he had with the managing director of the team, David Pitchforth."David said, 'Tony, it was definitely real because when they came to the office with it, I picked the diamond up, went to the window and scratched the window' because that's how to tell."Hearing that from Dave, I'm in no doubt it was the real thing that was put on the car."I don't know if one of our mechanics was switched on enough to make a fake, but I don't think so."Theory: someone pocketed it"I think somebody probably just picked it up, put it in their pocket and... they're probably smiling and thinking, 'it's in my drawer'," says Purnell."I do think also that a fairly large diamond zooming through at 100 miles an hour probably shattered. Somebody's got a little bit, somebody else has got another [little bit]."Maybe, sadly, just some guy was sweeping up the road or one of those trucks with the brushes and it all went down the sewer."It did occur to me that the ultimate thing would be if Clooney, Pitt and Damon had contrived to steal it because it was so in line with Ocean's Eleven. But that was a fantasy too far."There would have been hundreds, if not thousands, of people in the area because within an hour or so of the end of the race the circuit would have been returned to public roads.   Sidhu is pretty certain about what happened to the diamond: "Someone's picked it up."What people tend to do is, believe it or not, pick up bits of tyre rubber, you know, claim that as Michael Schumacher's front tyre rubber or whatever they can find."Somebody may have picked it up not having any idea it came off a car."There's a lot of diamonds in Monte Carlo. There's a lot of people walking around Monte Carlo with a lot of jewellery and a lot of stones."Somebody dropped a diamond in Monte Carlo. Well, they're not going to miss that, are they? Probably not."Theory: Klien crashed on purposeSidhu says the cost of the damage to the car was more than the cost of the diamond, which reports at the time said was uninsured.And points and a good result in the race were more valuable to the team and individuals than a diamond or the publicity a crash would bring. It was simply not worth crashing on purpose."For us, bringing two cars home, ideally in the points, had far bigger commercial benefits to us in terms of constructors' points, broadcast money, and more importantly, trying to retain our sponsors and trying to protect the integrity of the team," Sidhu explains.Klien drove straight into the barriers right in front of the marshals so would not have had the chance to start looking for a diamond or picking it up even if he had wanted to."Christian didn't try and say all the brakes failed or anything like that, he's just said 'I made a rookie mistake'," says Purnell."He was a young guy, first time, made a mistake, it happens. Doesn't usually happen with a $300,000 diamond flying into the crowd or wherever it went, but I'm sure Christian wasn't really aware of the diamond."No amount of money would have got Christian to do that [crash on purpose]. He wanted to make a success of what he was doing."While events were unfolding, Purnell had not really been thinking about the diamond. His main concern that day was that one of his drivers had crashed and the other also did not finish, and that this was not a good look in terms of pleasing current backers or attracting potential buyers."When Christian went into the wall and then later Mark retired, my entire thinking was 'Oh God. What am I going to say?' The chairman of HSBC [Jaguar's then sponsors] was there, Sir John Bond. Jackie [Stewart] was there."It was all about 'how am I going to explain another bad performance? How am I going to say 'just stick with the plan? We know what we're doing, it will take time' because sponsors don't have time. They want success."In the end, the missing diamond came to the rescue."No-one mentioned Jarno Trulli winning the Grand Prix, no-one asked how the Jaguars did. No-one was interested that Mark Webber's car broke as well. It was, 'where's the diamond?'" says Purnell."I remember talking to somebody in Detroit saying, 'fantastic publicity over here, you know we never hear anything about Formula 1 but it's on the newscasts, it's in the papers - fantastic'."Asked if the diamond mystery had helped the eventual sale of the team to Red Bull six months later, he replies: "I think that helped quite a lot because it buzzed the Jaguar team and showed that huge publicity was possible even if you weren't doing so well."Red Bull went on to become hugely successful, winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' championships since joining F1."You couldn't design a better PR weekend," says Purnell.Even if it was not quite how it was planned and there is still the small matter of a missing diamond.

title: Mauricio Pochettino tactics: Can Argentine solve Man Utd's problems?
description: How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man UtdImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Maurucio Pochettino (right) was f
body: How Ferguson-inspired Pochettino can succeed where Carrick failed at Man UtdImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Maurucio Pochettino (right) was first mentioned as a contender to manage Manchester United when Louis van Gaal was sacked in May 2016ByFootball tactics correspondentUpdated 3 hours agoWhen Mauricio Pochettino was asked the three Premier League managers he would have loved to have played for, he was unequivocal."Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Alex Ferguson," replied Pochettino, who on Friday was named Manchester United manager.In 2023, the Argentine - then at Chelsea, and dressed in full Blues training gear - was being interviewed by Sky Sports. Still he felt a need to express his adoration for Ferguson.Six years prior to that interview, while managing Tottenham, he had shared lunch with the legendary former United manager."When I was young, when I started my career as a manager, he was always my inspiration, my reference," Pochettino said. "And when you can share two hours with a person who was the greatest manager in the history of football, you can only enjoy."Hiring United managers has been complicated since Ferguson's departure in 2013, and one of the most prominent complications has been a back-and-forth around the club's DNA.For some, winning by any means necessary should take precedence, while others believe the style of play and cultural heritage of United's most successful period is vital to the club's identity.In recent years, United's managerial merry-go-round has alternated between European coaches with their own fixed styles of play, and former players from the Ferguson era.But between his tactics of choice and his adoration for the former United boss, Pochettino may be uniquely placed to bridge the gap between both camps.Michael Carrick's United produced a series of good results to finish last season with a run unmatched by any other team in the league. They looked great, but it was a greatness built on attacking in a transition-heavy manner. Under Carrick, in games they had less than 50% of the ball, they only lost once. In those 13 games, they boasted a win-rate of 62%. This dropped to 36% in games they had the majority of possession.This style of play suited their direct attackers and protected their defenders. At the same time, Casemiro's set-piece prowess provided United a reliable way to break the deadlock against deep defences - something they have struggled with this season. With United a goal up, opponents stepped forward, giving Carrick's men more space. They could play to their strengths again, attacking quickly. It worked.But teams at the top are reluctant to play in this way. Carrick's vision for United was a side that played slick football, with short passes in build-up intuitively, referencing Paris St-Germain's midfield three as a source of inspiration. Building up in this manner, to entice and escape from pressure, before looking to find the forwards quickly, was the plan Carrick was working towards.This didn't come to fruition and trying to take United from a successful counter-attacking side to one that could reliably beat teams while keeping the ball was the same hurdle that undid Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Erik ten Hag. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Former players under Sir Alex Ferguson, both Ole Gunnar Solskjar and Michael Carrick leaned into United’s historic style when crafting their game-modelsPochettino gives United an interesting solution to this problem.In his own words, he has described his sides as needing "to be protagonists, always press high, work hard and be dynamic". He refers to himself as a "disciple" of the legendary Argentina boss Marcelo Bielsa, who he played for. If you wanted an immediate comparison in the Premier League to a coach who resembles Pochettino's ideas in possession, it would be worth looking at Liverpool's  Andoni Iraola, who similarly cites Bielsa as his reference.These are coaches who, while taking the initiative, encourage vertical football. For as different as the clubs are, both the fans of United and Liverpool have enjoyed success when their teams have played high-octane football.This summer's World Cup was a strong showcase of Pochettino's style of play and his recent tactical adaptation. Rather than a fixed, positional style of play - akin to the work of somebody like Manchester City's Enzo Maresca - Pochettino's USA had only certain players being tasked with holding their position.This approach posed problems for teams who defended in a zonal manner - defending specific areas rather than individual players.The US midfielders being able to move freely meant they could step into areas of the pitch between the zones that were being defended, which resulted in their players often being unmarked with time and space on the ball.By playing in close proximity to each other in the middle of the pitch, the US found another benefit. Small-space passing combinations helped draw the opposing team up towards the ball and combined with clever off-ball movement to stretch the pitch, allowed the US to find their striker with few defenders around him.Pochettino's men looked to thread through-balls in behind and early after enticing the opposition's press and the speedy Folarin Balogun was able to turn those chances into goals.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage caption, Here is a good example of USA's fluid midfield four under Pochettino. The right-sided midfielder McKennie has placed himself near his three midfield team-mates, leaving the right half-space empty. With a four against three in that area of the pitch, USA are best placed to play quick combinations before looking to find their attackers in space.Slide 1 of 2, Screen grab showing USA’s tactics against Paraguay in the World Cup., Here is a good example of USA's fluid midfield four under Pochettino. The right-sided midfielder McKennie has placed himself near his three midfield team-mates, leaving the right half-space empty. With a four against three in that area of the pitch, USA are best placed to play quick combinations before looking to find their attackers in space.This combination of a fluid midfield, small-space passing and direct through-balls doesn't sound dissimilar to what Carrick was trying to move towards implementing this season. And although that may worry United fans, the similarity in principles will benefit the players. "My philosophy is to give a freer style with a good organisation," were Pochettino's words in 2014. Although philosophically similar, that latter part - a clearer organisation to his freer style - is likely to be what Carrick was unable to reliably offer his players. For fans of top sides, fast-paced, vertical football tends to be accepted when it comes from a place of being proactive - think Ferguson's United or Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool - wanting to keep the ball, but not passing it for passing's sake. Fast-paced, vertical football tends to be frowned upon when it comes from a place of conceding possession and defending your own goal for long periods of the match.The first half of Carrick's stint did appear proactive, while his 4-2-4 press worked well. Leaving four players high was a risk that allowed them to win the ball back and score quickly, but as teams figured this out, United failed to adapt. There also appeared to be a drop in the team's fitness the longer United went from the departure of ex-boss Ruben Amorim, who left United well conditioned, albeit on the back of a schedule without European football.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Here we see United's narrow 4-2-4 defensive shape in the first half against ComoHiring Pochettino will immediately begin the process of turning United into a well-drilled side, capable of applying intense pressure, likely in a co-ordinated manner. Pochettino enjoyed relative success with Spurs, built on this intensity and co-ordination, that differentiated him from the rest of the league. With that unique selling point more common now than a decade ago, how he builds on it will dictate how his tenure unfolds. But watching Brighton this season, he can be assured that an approach founded on intensity off the ball can work in the Premier League in 2026, with Fabian Hurzeler's men second in the league, with the fourth highest average possession, 10 games in.Pochettino, from a footballing point of view, feels extremely aligned to the values of Ferguson's United, and as a result will implement numerous similarities to the things Carrick wanted, but ultimately failed, to deliver. His wealth of experience make him a more proven entity than the departing United manager and if he can get his team fit and pressing high, in typically Pochettino fashion, they should see an upturn in form.Expanding on his managerial approach, while managing Spurs he explained how "the most important thing [was] to create a good shape for players to be comfortable and to show their real qualities".Rather than relying on pre-defined pattern, he looks to empower individuals to solve attacking problems. Taking this approach means recruitment of top talent matters more than ever."He [gave] me the confidence and licence to go where I wanted on the pitch, where I [could] use my strengths," said Cole Palmer, who enjoyed his most productive Premier League season under Pochettino at Chelsea.United have good attackers but they will need to take the same initiative Palmer did, if platformed to their strengths - something Pochettino does well.If they don't, and if Pochettino is to stumble, it will likely be in United's inability to break down stubborn defences when asked to dominate the ball - in what would feel like Groundhog Day, again.

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino tactics: Can Argentine solve Man Utd's problems?

title: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site
description: The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.Iran infor
body: The UN's nuclear watchdog has said it is "increasingly concerned" about a nuclear facility in Iran which it has not been allowed to inspect.Iran informed the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) of plans to set up the uranium enrichment plant in the city of Isfahan a day before Israel began attacking its nuclear sites last June. The US joined the strikes later that month.In a report seen by news agencies, the IAEA said it does not know the exact location or whether it contains nuclear material. Since the start of the latest war, Iran has restricted IAEA inspectors' access to its nuclear sites, preventing the agency from verifying its enriched uranium stockpile.Under a 2015 nuclear deal, Iran agreed to limit its enriched uranium stockpile to 300kg and enrichment to 3.67% purity. It subsequently exceeded both.Before the June 2025 strikes, it had accumulated an estimated 441kg enriched to 60%, close to weapons grade.The nuclear complex at Isfahan suffered extensive damage in US and Israeli strikes, particularly the parts above the ground. The condition of its underground facilities is not clear.The IAEA believes much of Iran's highly enriched uranium was stored there."The Agency's lack of information about [Iran's] nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said in the latest report.Iran announced plans for the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) on 12 June 2025, shortly after an IAEA resolution which declared Iran had failed to meet its nuclear safeguards obligations.Iran initially agreed to allow inspectors to visit the facility, but the inspection was cancelled after Israel launched attacks the following day.The IAEA's latest calls come almost a year after it made a similar appeal to Iran. At the time it said it had only inspected some of the 13 nuclear facilities that were "unaffected" by the attacks and none of the seven that were.The US and Israel said they attacked Iran's nuclear sites to prevent it developing nuclear weapons - something Iran has consistently denied seeking. It says its nuclear programme is for peaceful civilian purposes only.

schema.headline: UN watchdog 'increasingly concerned' over uninspected Iran nuclear site

title: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue
description: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The site of a car explosion which wounded Sergei Zavorotni in Moscow on FridayByDan SalesA car bomb in Moscow has
body: Image source, ReutersImage caption, The site of a car explosion which wounded Sergei Zavorotni in Moscow on FridayByDan SalesA car bomb in Moscow has injured a former adviser to Ukraine's pro-Putin ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.Sergei Zavorotny was behind the wheel when the explosion happened on Friday morning. He was taken to hospital, investigators added.Zavorotny had been an aide to Azarov until the prime minister resigned in 2014 and fled to Russia. The car bomb went off a day after a similar explosion killed a Russian colonel in Saint Petersburg.It comes against a backdrop of peace talks in Dublin aimed at ending the war, although strikes by both Russia and Ukraine continued overnight."Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Prime Minister of Ukraine Mykola Azarov, who was driving a car, was injured. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care," a statement from the committee said on Telegram."A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."Unconfirmed reports from Russia claim he has lost his left arm and suffered a brain injury, broken ribs and right leg.On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of Saint Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military.Russia say the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.Overnight Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.Ukraine say these are retaliatory attacks over Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.Image source, Sputnik / Pool via AFPImage caption, Witkoff and Kushner's visit to Moscow was the latest of many trips the US envoys have made to see Vladimir PutinThis week has seen informal peace talks in Dublin at a military airbase.US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff earlier had spoken with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.On Thursday in Dublin, Kushner said Putin was willing to accept European input in the peace process.On Friday, Taoiseach Micheál Martin said that European voice could not be confined to just member states - paving the way for the UK to have a role.Ahead of an informal meeting of the EU Council, he said: "The discussions today will focus perhaps both on the content and the type of peace that Europe wants to secure, the sustainable peace, and then also in terms of there will be discussion, obviously, in terms of who represents Europe."Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has welcomed the pledge of European involvement.Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022 and about a fifth of the country is now under occupation.Continued efforts to broker peace have failed so far, despite intensive talks.On Thursday Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that UK national security adviser Jonathan Powell would join Zelensky, Witkoff and Kushner for talks in Dublin.But hours later Downing Street said they had been delayed, which meant that the national security adviser could no longer join the meetings.

schema.headline: Russia hit by second car bomb in as many days as peace talks continue

title: MI5 will need proof to be believed in future, Leveson says following BBC investigation
description: The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of MI5 has said it will now have to provide proof to be believed by judges, after a BBC News investigat
body: The man responsible for overseeing the conduct of MI5 has said it will now have to provide proof to be believed by judges, after a BBC News investigation exposed how the security service lied to three courts.Lord Leveson, the investigatory powers commissioner and a former Court of Appeal justice, said that as a judge "if the security service said something to me, then I would accept it".But he said courts would now be "far more reluctant to accept, without evidential proof, things that are said in the future".Lord Leveson praised the impact of the BBC's investigation into an abusive MI5 agent, which he said had led to changes in how informants are managed.He spoke to the BBC during the first annual conference of the Investigatory Powers Commissioner's Office (Ipco).The BBC's investigation had "hit the intelligence community hard", including security services around the world, he said.The BBC investigation exposed how a neo-Nazi informant - known as Agent X - used his state role as a tool of abuse. He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. He had previously abused another woman and threatened to kill her child.Despite all this, MI5 protected the agent and helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while he was under police investigation, even removing his possessions from a police station.In his first interview about the case, Lord Leveson said he stood ready to assist the police if asked.He said that "MI5 have a great distance to go" with courts in the future.He added the BBC investigation's reach "has been far greater than if this had never happened. So you can take some pride in that."Lord Leveson said there was also a change in the way that agents, also known as covert human intelligence sources (CHIS), were managed.Because of the Agent X case, there is a new policy relating to agents and domestic violence, and coercive control."There is no doubt that concern is now being focused not merely on the activity of the CHIS, but the impact of the CHIS on other aspects of his or her life. "I think that everybody learns from disasters, and this for MI5 has been a very serious matter."The Ipco chief executive, Richard Thompson, now attends meetings of an internal board in MI5, created to oversee changes because of the Agent X case, including changes in culture within the service.In addition, MI5 must change the way it prepares and gives evidence, after the High Court case.Lord Leveson said intelligence service chiefs from around the world had contacted him about the case.They had expressed concern about whether something similar could happen in their organisations, he said.The Agent X case had "done a great service to everybody", Lord Leveson saidThe Ipco investigation examined how MI5 gave false evidence to three courts about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) - about the agent status of the violent neo-Nazi informant.The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block our investigation into Agent X, but won him legal anonymity. His ex-partner Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.MI5 claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from Beth and everyone else, leaving her at a serious disadvantage.But what MI5 said was untrue. It had, in fact, disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.A senior MI5 officer had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist. He even wanted me to meet the agent. In doing so, he repeatedly departed from the NCND policy.That officer was found to have repeatedly lied by the IPCO investigation. He has resigned from MI5 since the BBC exposed what happened.

schema.headline: MI5 will need proof to be believed in future, Leveson says following BBC investigation

title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
description: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.Pharmacies and businesses have also be
body: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime. Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need. A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts."Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.Elsewhere:Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normalMPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in placeThe Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outageMSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent caseworkSome businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage.The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain."Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained. "Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here."He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others"."Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge."His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption.Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed."We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.
